103: TGN kept a running node memory. TGAT instead rebuilds a representation from retrieved events; the new question is how elapsed time changes attention.
An embedding is a vector representing an entity. Attention forms a weighted sum of neighbor vectors. A cutoff is the time beyond which a query cannot read records.
Audit which records actually entered that representation.
104: A temporal encoder can process timestamps while still reading forbidden records. Trace the data dependencies before trusting its score.
Event time says when something happened; availability time says when the predictor could read it. A label is the outcome to predict, not an input feature.
Ask what a daily snapshot discards even when its inputs are legal.
105: Legal history still needs a representation. Compare individual events with completed windows before selecting a model.
A snapshot summarizes one interval. Two repeated interactions are two events, even if a binary adjacency stores only one edge. Half-open [a,b) includes a but excludes b.
Define the candidate interactions against which a prediction will be scored.
106: The representation alone does not define the test. Fix the positive questions and sampled negative candidates before judging a scorer.

A positive is an observed interaction. A negative is a comparison under a declared sampling rule. Precision measures how many selected candidates are positive; recall measures how many positives were selected.
Choose which state a model carries between completed snapshots.
107: EdgeBank remembered pairs. A learned snapshot model needs a precise answer to a new question: does history live in node states or in convolution weights?
A GCN mixes neighboring features within one graph. A recurrent update combines new input with stored state across time. These are separate directions of computation.
Retrieve a bounded event history without confusing a faster implementation with a changed sampler.
108: Snapshot aggregation saved work by discarding timing. Temporal sampling keeps event records but limits how many a query reads.
Fanout counts sampled neighbor slots per hop. A hop follows one relationship. Padding fills missing slots and must not be mistaken for a real historical event.
Decide which database timestamps can actually support those cutoffs.
109: A fast temporal sampler assumes that timestamps mean what its predicates say. A database column name does not establish that meaning.
A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key names a related row. An as-of join reconstructs the versions usable at a historical cutoff before following those keys.
Carry the information contract through training and checkpoint restoration.
110: The clock, sampler and model are now defined. The checkpoint must preserve the predictor that actually produced the selected validation score.
Parameters are learned shared weights. Temporal state includes memories, clocks and pending messages. A checkpoint is a saved state; restoring only some of it can change predictions.
Transfer this protocol discipline to an official static-graph benchmark.
112: Lesson 111 fixes the official questions and evaluator. Now replace its simple baseline with the complete published GCN training procedure.
Transductive means held-out feature rows and graph structure can participate while held-out labels are excluded from loss. A percentage point is an absolute difference between percentages.
Determine what changes when a full graph no longer fits one training step.
113: The full-graph GCN provides a reference computation. Scaling requires separating the sampling rule from the model that consumes the sampled graph.
An induced subgraph retains all edges whose endpoints are selected. GraphSAGE combines root and neighbor transforms; it is not the same operator as symmetrically normalized GCN.
Return to arxiv and identify which populations the trained model gets wrong.
114: Scaling answered how to run a model. Error analysis asks where its predictions fail, using explicit denominators and fixed comparison questions.
A slice is a subset selected by a stated rule. Degree counts neighbors. Homophily measures neighbor-label agreement; using true labels for diagnosis does not make them available at prediction time.
Describe a proposed change in terms of encoder, processor and prediction head.
115: The error report motivates changes. Module contracts let us say precisely which computation changes and which should remain equivalent.
An encoder turns inputs into vectors; a processor exchanges information; a head produces the requested outputs. Pooling reduces several node vectors to one graph vector.
Probe whether the implemented modules and optimizer fulfill those contracts.
116: A modular design can still train incorrectly. Use a small experiment to separate competing explanations of the same symptom.
A gradient describes loss sensitivity. The optimizer uses it to change parameters. A finite gradient does not prove that an update happened or that row identities are correct.
Build the graph from database keys rather than accepting it as a given.
117: You can now design and debug a GNN. Relational learning adds the missing input question: how do database rows become a query-specific graph?
A schema describes tables and key roles. A relational entity graph contains actual rows and key links. A computation graph contains the sampled occurrences used for one prediction.
Compare this modern stack with the earlier target-specific extraction and readout in Cvitkovic.
118: The modern RDL bridge motivates a look backward. Compare extraction and readout choices rather than treating publication date as a ranking.
A target-specific graph is the context selected for one prediction. Table-specific encoders can feed a convolution whose weights are shared across all relation types.
Turn representation mechanisms and their limitations into a defensible synthesis.
119: The two relational constructions expose useful choices. Now separate information preserved by a representation, functions a model can express, and evidence from a measured experiment.
A collision means different inputs become identical features. No deterministic predictor using only those features can give the two inputs different answers.
Demonstrate the complete pipeline and defend it in the Year 3 exit exam.
120: The synthesis made a conditional argument for relational learning. The exam asks you to make the supporting graph, clock, training and evaluation contracts executable.
Query identity includes entity and cutoff. Local tensor position, database row identity and query ownership are different indices. Context rows can receive gradients without receiving direct labels.
Use the historical map to understand why the Year 4 design choices exist.
121: After assembling the pipeline, locate its choices among rules, engineered aggregates and learned message passing. The historical detour explains alternatives you must compare fairly.
An aggregate reduces a group of values, such as a sum per order. Changing the grouping can change the answer even when all original values remain present.
Construct the row graph and verify every edge against a relational join.
122: The historical comparison showed that representation matters. Start the modern pipeline by preserving row identities and relationship roles exactly.
Raw keys name entities; local indices address tensor rows. An edge tensor has a sender row and a receiver row. Reverse relations change message direction, not the original database fact.
Restrict each prediction to the rows visible at its own cutoff.
123: Correct key mapping does not prevent future context. Construct a separate legal neighborhood for each entity-time question.
A seed is the entity being predicted. A node occurrence is its copy inside one sampled query graph. Here every hop uses the root cutoff; TGAT in L103 used decreasing child cutoffs.
Specify the future target and identify each question in a task table.
124: The legal context is defined, but it does not say what to predict. A task table connects entity-time questions to future outcomes.
An entity row describes one object. A task row describes one prediction request. A prediction horizon defines the future interval from which its label is built.
Turn the allowed mixed-type feature columns into trainable row vectors.
125: We have rows, relationships and prediction requests. Row encoding supplies the numerical vectors that message passing needs.
A semantic type describes how a column is interpreted. Materialization applies a fitted vocabulary or statistic; trainable encoding maps that prepared value into a vector.
Use the benchmark API to keep database inputs, task questions and evaluation aligned.
126: The individual data transformations now need a shared evaluation interface. Keep the database, prediction task and evaluator separate.
An evaluator compares aligned predictions and labels. Matching array lengths is insufficient: entity IDs and cutoffs must refer to the same questions in the same order.
Freeze the entire neural training and selection protocol for RelBench v1.
127: The API can score answers. A reproducible neural experiment also fixes architecture, fitting, checkpoint selection and aggregation across runs.
Validation chooses a checkpoint. Test evaluates that frozen choice. Seed standard deviation describes variation among fits on this fixed task; it is not variation across databases.
Change head, loss and metric when the prediction request changes.
128: One regression result is not a universal task template. Let the query and outcome determine whether you need a number, a probability or a ranking.
A logit is an unconstrained score. A probability describes a binary outcome under its task contract. A recommendation score orders a declared candidate set.
Construct the strong feature-engineered competitor under the same question contract.
129: The task taxonomy fixes what to predict. Manual feature engineering is a serious competing way to expose the same relational information.
An as-of feature uses only permitted history at the query cutoff. A boosted tree adds successive fitted corrections. Feature design time and machine training time are different costs.
Assemble the complete RDL pipeline and defend it against this comparison.
130: The baseline and competitor are available. The checkpoint tests ownership of the complete chain from a database query to an independently verified result.
MAE is the mean absolute prediction error, in target units. A prediction packet must preserve entity and cutoff keys so independently saved outputs can be aligned.
Instrument a real forward and backward pass to explain what is learned.
131: A working pipeline still leaves its internal computation hidden. Follow one real batch through row encoding, time addition, messages, root readout and gradients.
A tensor shape counts rows and coordinates. Autograd records differentiable operations. Detaching a tensor preserves its current values but cuts its gradient path.
Ask how representations can depend on which entity is the current query root.
132: The traced stack encodes table type and time. Recommendation also needs to preserve who is asking while scoring candidate entities.
A root marker is one shared vector identifying the query role. It differs from a separately learned vector for each global ID. A two-tower model scores source and destination vectors together.
Open the relation-specific arithmetic that combines all those messages.
133: Root identity tells us whose question is being answered. The next step is to reconstruct exactly what each incoming relation contributes to one row.
Sum within a relation combines neighbor vectors. Sum across relations combines complete relation outputs, including their root transforms and biases. Empty edges and an absent relation key differ.
Budget the sampled occurrences while preserving this layer computation.
134: The layer equation is fixed. Scaling decides which query-owned occurrences reach it and measures the resulting computation.

Throughput is completed queries divided by elapsed time. GPU allocated memory tracks live tensors; reserved memory also includes allocator-held space. Fanout gives an expansion bound, not measured memory.
Use the measured costs to reserve and enforce a fair tuning budget in Lesson 135.
